error_modes.label: Touch down point control after the instrument-to-visual transition (FLAPS LDG / FLAPS T-O / AOA)
error_modes.source: specific:TOUCH DOWN POINT (feet from the beginning of the RWY) [a/ FLAPS LDG - FLAPS T/O - AOA]

texts.0: SP, due to a late and shallow round out flown with residual power after breaking out of the approach, did not fly the aircraft to the projected touch down point. The aircraft floated in ground effect and contacted the runway more than 1500 feet beyond the projected touch down point, well outside the plus/minus 1000 feet limit. IP intervened on power and pitch to stop the landing being extended further into the remaining runway.
texts.1: SP, due to an unstabilized final segment after the transition to visual flight, did not adjust power to hold the aim point on the projected touch down point. Touch down occurred approximately 1000 feet long, at the plus/minus 1000 feet limit, and only after repeated verbal prompting from IP to reduce power. The correction was applied so late that the deviation was contained rather than removed.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly high energy state carried into the visual segment, initially tracked above the glidepath toward the projected touch down point. SP recognized the trend, reduced power and re-established the aim point without any intervention from IP. Touch down occurred about 700 feet from the projected touch down point, between the 500 and 1000 feet standards.
texts.3: SP transitioned smoothly to visual flight and flew a stabilized aim point onto the projected touch down point. Power and pitch were adjusted in small, timely increments and the aircraft touched down within 500 feet of the projected touch down point. Aim point control on the visual segment required no prompting from IP.
texts.4: SP arrived at the visual segment on speed and on glidepath and placed the aircraft on the projected touch down point with negligible error. Touch down occurred within approximately 100 feet of the projected point, with no float and no late power change. Aim point control was equally precise on each repetition of the maneuver.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within the 500 feet standard from the projected touch down point, but consistently on the long side of it and after a small float on each attempt. The trend of carrying a few extra knots into the round out is currently absorbed by the runway available, which would not be the case on a shorter or contaminated surface. SP is expected to set the aim point earlier and to reduce power to idle at the correct height so that the touch down point is centered rather than long.

texts_at.0: SP flew the visual segment with the IP flying the aim point correction for the projected touch down point on the first approach and calling the power reduction for SP to fly on the second. Adjusting power for the aim point the moment visual flight begins has not yet been learned. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to adjust power for the aim point independently as the visual segment becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP flew the visual segment with touch down settling at approximately 1000 feet from the projected point, due to an unstabilized final segment after the transition to visual flight. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to adjust power for the aim point the moment visual flight begins, not partway through the segment.
texts_at.2: SP flew the visual segment with touch down settling at about 700 feet from the projected point, due to a slightly high energy state carried into the visual segment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power the instant the high energy state is recognized rather than tracking above the glidepath first.
texts_at.3: SP transitioned smoothly to visual flight and flew a stabilized aim point onto the projected touch down point within 500 feet, due to power and pitch being adjusted a fraction later than ideal on one approach. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the power and pitch adjustment at the same point on every approach as consistently as the others.

texts_above.1: SP flew the visual segment with touch down settling at approximately 1000 feet from the projected point before the aim point was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the aim point. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend, reduced power and re-established the aim point without any intervention from IP, after touch down had settled at about 700 feet from the projected point. Reducing power the instant the high energy state is recognized, rather than tracking above the glidepath first, would bring that point closer to the aim point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good aim-point technique.
texts_above.3: SP transitioned smoothly to visual flight and flew a stabilized aim point onto the projected touch down point, with power and pitch adjusted in small, timely increments and touch down within 500 feet of the projected point. The only refinement available is to make the power and pitch adjustment at the same point on every approach as consistently as the others. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good aim-point technique.
texts_above.4: SP arrived at the visual segment on speed and on glidepath and placed the aircraft on the projected touch down point with negligible error, within approximately 100 feet, with no float and no late power change. There is little left to refine; the aim point is already accurate rather than corrected into. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent aim-point technique.

error_modes.label: Touch down point control in the flaps up landing (FLAPS UP)
error_modes.source: specific:TOUCH DOWN POINT (feet from the beginning of the RWY) [b/ FLAPS UP]

texts.0: SP, due to flying the flaps up visual segment with the same power setting used for a flaps landing configuration, did not account for the reduced drag and the flatter deck angle. The aircraft floated well down the runway and touched down more than 1600 feet from the projected touch down point, outside the plus/minus 1000 feet limit. IP took the controls to prevent the landing rollout starting from an unacceptable point on the runway.
texts.1: SP, due to an unstabilized final in the flaps up configuration, did not establish a fixed aim point after the transition to visual flight. The aircraft touched down approximately 1000 feet from the projected touch down point, at the plus/minus 1000 feet limit, after IP directed a power reduction on short final. Without that verbal direction the deviation would have continued to develop.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly flat approach path in the flaps up configuration, initially tracked short of the projected touch down point. SP identified the shallow path, added power to regain the glidepath and re-established the aim point without intervention from IP. Touch down occurred about 600 feet from the projected touch down point, between the 500 and 1000 feet standards.
texts.3: SP flew the flaps up visual segment with the correct higher approach speed and a stable aim point on the projected touch down point. Power was reduced progressively through the round out and the aircraft touched down within 500 feet of the projected point. The reduced drag of the configuration was correctly anticipated.
texts.4: SP compensated precisely for the flaps up configuration and placed the aircraft on the projected touch down point with negligible error. Touch down occurred within approximately 150 feet of the projected point, with no float and no correction required on short final. The result was repeated consistently.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within the 500 feet standard, but each flaps up landing developed toward the long side after a noticeable float in ground effect. The trend indicates that the idle selection is being made slightly high and late for this configuration, and the margin is being provided by runway length rather than by technique. SP is expected to anticipate the lower drag of the flaps up configuration and to time the power reduction so that the touch down point is centered on the projected point.

texts_at.0: SP flew the flaps up visual segment with the IP flying the aim point correction for the projected touch down point on the first approach and calling the power reduction for SP to fly on the second. Establishing a fixed aim point in the flaps up configuration has not yet been learned. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to establish the fixed aim point independently as the configuration becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP flew the flaps up visual segment with touch down settling at approximately 1000 feet from the projected point, due to an unstabilized final in the flaps up configuration. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to establish a fixed aim point the moment the field is in sight, not partway down the visual segment.
texts_at.2: SP flew the flaps up visual segment with touch down settling at about 600 feet from the projected point, due to a slightly flat approach path in the flaps up configuration. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to add power the instant the path is recognized as flat rather than letting it develop further.
texts_at.3: SP flew the flaps up visual segment with the correct higher approach speed and a stable aim point, touching down within 500 feet of the projected point, due to power reduced a fraction later than ideal through the round out. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to time the power reduction the same way on every flaps up landing.

texts_above.1: SP flew the flaps up visual segment with touch down settling at approximately 1000 feet from the projected point before the aim point was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the aim point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP identified the shallow path, added power to regain the glidepath and re-established the aim point without intervention from IP, after touch down had trended to about 600 feet from the projected point. Adding power the instant the path is recognized as flat, rather than letting it develop, would bring that point closer to the aim point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound flaps-up aim-point technique.
texts_above.3: SP flew the flaps up visual segment with the correct higher approach speed and a stable aim point on the projected touch down point, with power reduced progressively through the round out and touch down within 500 feet of the projected point. The only refinement available is to time the power reduction the same way on every flaps up landing. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed flaps-up aim-point technique.
texts_above.4: SP compensated precisely for the flaps up configuration and placed the aircraft on the projected touch down point with negligible error, within approximately 150 feet, with no float and no correction required on short final. There is little left to refine; the lower drag of the configuration is already anticipated rather than corrected for. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional flaps-up aim-point technique.

error_modes.label: Runway centerline tracking at touch down (FLAPS LDG / FLAPS T-O / AOA)
error_modes.source: specific:DEVIATION FROM CENTER LINE (feet) [a/ FLAPS LDG - FLAPS T/O - AOA]

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete lateral alignment when transitioning from the approach course to the visual runway picture, did not use rudder to place the aircraft on the runway centerline before touch down. The aircraft contacted the runway more than 20 feet from the centerline with residual drift, outside the plus/minus 15 feet limit. IP intervened on rudder and aileron to recover alignment during the initial rollout.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed lateral correction after breaking out of the approach, did not complete the alignment with the runway centerline during the round out. Touch down occurred approximately 15 feet from the centerline, at the limit, and only after IP called for rudder. The lateral trend was stopped by the prompt rather than by SP's own scan of the runway picture.
texts.2: SP, due to a small lateral offset carried over from the approach course, initially tracked to one side of the runway centerline in the visual segment. SP recognized the offset, applied rudder and aileron and closed most of it before touch down, contacting the runway about 10 feet from the centerline, between the 5 and 15 feet standards. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP transitioned to the visual runway picture and aligned the aircraft with the centerline in a single smooth correction. Touch down occurred within 5 feet of the centerline with the longitudinal axis parallel to the runway and no residual drift. Directional control during the initial rollout was positive.
texts.4: SP arrived on the visual segment already aligned with the runway centerline and maintained that alignment through the round out. Touch down occurred within approximately 2 feet of the centerline with no lateral correction required at any point. Alignment was maintained throughout the rollout without deviation.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within the 5 feet standard from the centerline, but consistently displaced to the same side and with the final alignment correction made low in the round out. The trend shows the lateral correction being deferred until the visual picture is very close rather than being made immediately after breaking out. SP is expected to complete the alignment earlier in the visual segment so that the round out is flown from an already centered position.

texts_at.0: SP flew the round out with the IP completing the lateral alignment with the runway centerline on the first landing and calling the reference for SP to hold on the second. Completing the lateral alignment the moment the visual runway picture is acquired has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to complete the lateral alignment independently as the picture becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP touched down with lateral deviation settling at approximately 15 feet from the centerline, due to an incomplete lateral alignment when transitioning from the approach course to the visual runway picture. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the lateral alignment the moment the visual runway picture is acquired, not during the round out.
texts_at.2: SP touched down with lateral deviation settling at about 10 feet from the centerline, due to a small lateral offset carried over from the approach course. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to correct any carried-over offset the instant the visual segment begins rather than during the round out.
texts_at.3: SP transitioned to the visual runway picture and aligned the aircraft with the centerline in a single smooth correction, touching down within 5 feet of the centerline, due to the correction being made a beat later than ideal on one approach. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make that single correction at the same point in the transition on every approach.

texts_above.1: SP touched down with lateral deviation settling at approximately 15 feet from the centerline before the alignment was completed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the drift. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the offset, applied rudder and aileron and closed most of it before touch down, contacting the runway about 10 feet from the centerline, without prompting or intervention. Correcting any carried-over offset the instant the visual segment begins, rather than during the round out, would close the remainder of that offset. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid centerline discipline at touch down.
texts_above.3: SP transitioned to the visual runway picture and aligned the aircraft with the centerline in a single smooth correction, touching down within 5 feet of the centerline with the longitudinal axis parallel to the runway. The only refinement available is to make that correction at the same point in the transition on every approach. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed centerline discipline at touch down.
texts_above.4: SP arrived on the visual segment already aligned with the runway centerline and maintained that alignment through the round out, touching down within approximately 2 feet of the centerline with no lateral correction required at any point. There is little left to refine; alignment is already established before the round out rather than during it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding centerline discipline at touch down.

error_modes.source: specific:DEVIATION FROM CENTER LINE (feet) [b/ FLAPS UP]

texts.0: SP, due to concentrating on the higher approach speed of the flaps up configuration, did not maintain lateral alignment with the runway centerline through the round out. texts.1: SP, due to a late lateral correction in the flaps up visual segment, did not place the aircraft on the runway centerline before contact. texts.2: SP, due to a lateral offset carried into the visual segment from the approach, initially tracked off the runway centerline in the flaps up configuration. SP detected the offset, corrected with rudder and closed most of it before touch down, contacting the runway about 9 feet from the centerline, between the 5 and 15 feet standards. The correction was made in time and without intervention.
texts.3: SP flew the flaps up visual segment aligned with the runway centerline and held that alignment through the flatter round out. texts.4: SP maintained runway centerline alignment throughout the flaps up visual segment with negligible lateral error. Touch down occurred within approximately 2 feet of the centerline with no correction required in the round out. The alignment was held unchanged through the rollout.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within the 5 feet standard from the centerline, but each flaps up landing drifted slowly to the same side during the extended float before contact. The trend indicates that lateral scanning is being reduced while attention is held on the higher touch down speed of this configuration. texts_at.1: SP touched down with lateral deviation settling at approximately 15 feet from the centerline, due to concentrating on the higher approach speed of the flaps up configuration. texts_at.3: SP flew the flaps up visual segment aligned with the runway centerline and held that alignment through the flatter round out, touching down within 5 feet of the centerline, due to the alignment needing a small correction a beat later than ideal. texts_above.1: SP touched down with lateral deviation settling at approximately 15 feet from the centerline before the alignment was completed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the drift. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.

The only refinement available is to hold the alignment with the same discipline as the standard configuration. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate flaps-up centerline discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained runway centerline alignment throughout the flaps up visual segment with negligible lateral error, touching down within approximately 2 feet of the centerline with no correction required in the round out. error_modes.label: Touch down speed control (FLAPS LDG / FLAPS T-O / AOA)
error_modes.source: specific:TOUCH DOWN SPEED (knots) [a/ FLAPS LDG - FLAPS T/O - AOA]

texts.0: SP, due to holding excess power through the round out after the transition to visual flight, did not decelerate the aircraft to the computed touch down speed. The wheels contacted the runway more than 12 knots above the computed speed, outside the -5 to +10 knots band, after an extended float. IP took the controls to arrest the developing bounce and to stop the resulting drift.
texts.1: SP, due to a rushed flare initiated from an unstabilized final, did not complete the deceleration to the computed touch down speed. The aircraft contacted the runway approximately 10 knots fast, at the upper limit of the -5 to +10 knots band, after IP called for the power to be brought to idle. The energy was contained by that call rather than by SP's own timing.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late idle selection in the round out, carried extra energy into the flare. SP recognized the float, held the landing attitude and allowed the aircraft to decelerate, touching down about 7 knots fast, between the +5 and +10 knots standards. No prompting or intervention from IP was required.
texts.3: SP reduced power at the correct height, held the landing attitude and allowed the aircraft to decelerate to the computed touch down speed. The wheels contacted the runway within the 0 to +5 knots band with no float and no bounce. Pitch and power were coordinated throughout the round out.
texts.4: SP managed the energy on the visual segment so that the aircraft arrived over the touch down point exactly on the computed speed. Touch down occurred within approximately 1 knot of the computed speed, in the correct landing attitude and with no float. The result was repeated on each landing.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within the 0 to +5 knots band, but at the fast end of it on every landing and after a short float each time. The trend of carrying additional speed into the round out consumes runway and reduces the margin available in a crosswind or on a wet surface. SP is expected to select idle at the correct height so that the touch down speed is centered in the band rather than at its upper edge.

texts_at.0: SP flew the round out with the IP reducing power at the correct height on the first landing and calling the height for SP to fly on the second. Reducing power at the correct height, rather than holding it through the round out, has not yet been learned. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to reduce power at the correct height independently as the picture becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP touched down with speed settling at approximately 10 knots fast, at the upper limit of the band, due to holding excess power through the round out after the transition to visual flight. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power at the correct height on every landing rather than holding it through the round out.
texts_at.2: SP touched down with speed settling at about 7 knots fast, between the +5 and +10 knots standards, due to a slightly late idle selection in the round out. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to select idle the instant the correct height is reached rather than a moment after.
texts_at.3: SP reduced power at the correct height, held the landing attitude and allowed the aircraft to decelerate to the computed touch down speed, contacting the runway within the 0 to +5 knots band, due to the idle selection being made a fraction later than ideal on one approach. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select idle at the same height on every landing as consistently as the others.

texts_above.1: SP touched down with speed settling at approximately 10 knots fast, at the upper limit of the band, before the aircraft decelerated further. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the height for the power reduction. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the float, held the landing attitude and allowed the aircraft to decelerate, touching down about 7 knots fast, without prompting or intervention. Selecting idle the instant the correct height is reached, rather than a moment after, would bring that speed closer to the reference. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable speed management at touch down.
texts_above.3: SP reduced power at the correct height, held the landing attitude and allowed the aircraft to decelerate to the computed touch down speed, with the wheels contacting the runway within the 0 to +5 knots band and no float and no bounce. The only refinement available is to select idle at the same height on every landing as consistently as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good speed management at touch down.
texts_above.4: SP managed the energy on the visual segment so the aircraft arrived over the touch down point exactly on the computed speed, within approximately 1 knot, in the correct landing attitude and with no float. There is little left to refine; the energy is already managed on the visual segment rather than corrected at the round out. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior speed management at touch down.

error_modes.label: Touch down speed control in the flaps up landing (FLAPS UP)

texts.0: SP, due to applying the flaps landing sight picture and flare timing to a flaps up landing, did not decelerate the aircraft to the computed flaps up touch down speed. The aircraft touched down more than 13 knots fast, outside the -5 to +10 knots band, after a prolonged float in ground effect. IP intervened on the controls to prevent a bounce and to stabilize the aircraft on the runway.
texts.1: SP, due to reducing power too late in the flaps up round out, did not complete the deceleration before contact. The wheels touched approximately 10 knots above the computed speed, at the upper limit of the -5 to +10 knots band, after IP directed the throttle to idle. Without that direction the float would have continued.
texts.2: SP, due to the lower drag of the flaps up configuration, initially decelerated more slowly than required in the round out. SP recognized the float, held the attitude and did not force the aircraft onto the runway, touching down about 8 knots fast, between the +5 and +10 knots standards. The correction was timely and required no intervention.
texts.3: SP flew the flaps up approach at the correct higher speed and reduced power so that the aircraft decelerated to the computed flaps up touch down speed. Contact occurred within the 0 to +5 knots band in the correct, flatter landing attitude with no float. The different drag characteristics of the configuration were correctly anticipated.
texts.4: SP managed the flaps up energy so precisely that the aircraft arrived over the touch down point on the computed speed. Touch down occurred within approximately 2 knots of the computed speed, with no float and no pitch correction in the round out. The technique was consistent across repetitions.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within the 0 to +5 knots band, but at the upper edge of it on each flaps up landing and after a longer float than the configuration requires. The trend indicates that the idle selection is being timed on the flaps landing sight picture rather than on the flaps up one. SP is expected to begin the power reduction earlier in the flaps up round out so that the touch down speed is centered in the band.

texts_at.0: SP flew the flaps up round out with the IP using the flaps up sight picture and flare timing on the first landing and calling the power reduction for SP to fly on the second. Using the flaps up sight picture and flare timing, rather than the flaps landing one, has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to use the flaps up sight picture and flare timing independently as the configuration becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP touched down with speed settling at approximately 10 knots fast, at the upper limit of the band, due to applying the flaps landing sight picture and flare timing to a flaps up landing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to use the flaps up sight picture and flare timing for the flaps up landing, not the flaps landing one.
texts_at.2: SP touched down with speed settling at about 8 knots fast, between the +5 and +10 knots standards, due to reducing power too late in the flaps up round out. texts_at.3: SP flew the flaps up approach at the correct higher speed and reduced power so the aircraft decelerated to the computed flaps up touch down speed, contacting within the 0 to +5 knots band, due to the power reduction beginning a fraction later than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin the reduction at the same point on every flaps up landing as consistently as the others.

texts_above.1: SP touched down with speed settling at approximately 10 knots fast, at the upper limit of the band, before the aircraft decelerated further. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the flaps up flare timing. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the float, held the attitude and did not force the aircraft onto the runway, touching down about 8 knots fast, without intervention. Beginning the power reduction earlier in the flaps up round out, rather than on the standard-configuration timing, would bring that speed closer to the reference. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured flaps-up speed management.
texts_above.3: SP flew the flaps up approach at the correct higher speed and reduced power so the aircraft decelerated to the computed flaps up touch down speed, with contact inside the 0 to +5 knots band in the correct, flatter landing attitude and no float. The only refinement available is to begin the reduction at the same point on every flaps up landing as consistently as the others. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise flaps-up speed management.
texts_above.4: SP managed the flaps up energy so precisely that the aircraft arrived over the touch down point on the computed speed, within approximately 2 knots, with no float and no pitch correction in the round out. There is little left to refine; the technique is already consistent across repetitions. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate flaps-up speed management.

error_modes.label: Smooth transition from instrument to visual flight without abrupt attitude change

texts.0: SP, due to a somatogravic sensation on looking outside at the end of the approach at night, did not transition smoothly from instrument to visual flight and made an abrupt nose down attitude change. The flight path departed the glidepath sharply and the aircraft arrived at the runway threshold low and fast, with the touch down point deviation exceeding 1000 feet. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the landing attitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a disorienting visual illusion at the transition to visual flight, did not maintain the aircraft attitude while changing the reference from the instruments to the outside picture. The pitch excursion that followed placed the aircraft at the plus/minus 1000 feet limit of the touch down point standard, and it was corrected only after IP called the attitude. The recovery was reactive rather than anticipated.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief disorientation at the change of visual reference on breaking out, made a small abrupt pitch input immediately after transitioning to visual flight. SP recognized the excursion at once, returned to the correct attitude by cross-checking the instruments and resumed the flight path, holding the touch down point between the 500 and 1000 feet standards. No intervention from IP was necessary.
texts.3: SP transitioned from instrument to visual flight without abrupt changes in aircraft attitude. The scan was expanded progressively from the instruments to the outside picture while pitch, bank and power were held stable, and the aircraft continued on the glidepath to the touch down point within 500 feet of the projected point. No disorientation effect was allowed to influence the control inputs.
texts.4: SP made the transition to visual flight so smoothly that no attitude change was discernible at the point of transition. The instrument cross-check was retained as a reference while the outside picture was acquired, and the flight path continued unchanged to a touch down within 500 feet of the projected point. Control of the aircraft was uninterrupted throughout.
texts.marginal: SP transitioned from instrument to visual flight within standards, but each transition was accompanied by a small pitch adjustment that indicates the outside picture is being accepted before it is fully resolved. The trend is more evident at night and in reduced visibility, when the illusion potential is highest and the available correction time is shortest. SP is expected to retain the instrument cross-check through the transition so that the attitude remains unchanged while the visual reference is acquired.

texts_at.0: SP flew the transition to visual flight with the IP holding the instrument cross-check through the transition on the first approach and calling the attitude for SP to hold on the second. Holding the instrument cross-check through the transition, so an illusion cannot influence pitch, has not yet been learned. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. error_modes.label: Positive and timely recognition of the runway environment

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of positional awareness relative to the runway on the final segment of the approach, did not identify the runway environment positively or in time. SP called the runway in sight while looking at another lighting feature and turned the aircraft away from the approach course, and the resulting lateral displacement exceeded 20 feet at the point where alignment should have been established. IP took the controls, identified the runway and continued the landing.
texts.1: SP, due to reduced awareness of position relative to the approach end, did not recognize the runway environment until well inside the normal transition point. The late acquisition compressed the visual segment and the landing was completed at the plus/minus 1000 feet limit of the touch down point standard, after IP pointed out the runway. texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete picture of the aircraft position relative to the runway, initially looked in the wrong sector on breaking out. No intervention or prompting was required.
texts.3: SP maintained awareness of the aircraft position throughout the approach and recognized the runway environment positively and in time. No assistance was needed at any stage.
texts.4: SP anticipated where the runway environment would appear, identified it immediately and unambiguously, and began the transition to visual flight at exactly the right moment. The visual segment was consequently unhurried, with the aircraft on speed, on glidepath and aligned to a touch down within 500 feet of the projected point. Awareness of position was complete throughout the approach.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the runway environment within standards, but the identification was hesitant and confirmed only after a second look on each approach. error_modes.label: Round out and float control on the visual segment
error_modes.source: general:a|specific:TOUCH DOWN POINT (feet from the beginning of the RWY)

texts.0: SP, due to initiating the round out at an incorrect height and continuing to raise the nose without reducing power, did not stabilize the landing attitude before contact. The aircraft ballooned, floated well past the projected touch down point and touched down more than 1500 feet from it, outside the plus/minus 1000 feet limit. IP took the controls to arrest the ballooning and to complete the landing.
texts.1: SP, due to a high round out flown with the throttle still advanced, did not establish and hold the landing attitude. The extended float produced a touch down approximately 1000 feet from the projected touch down point, at the plus/minus 1000 feet limit, and the attitude was stabilized only after IP called for the pitch and the power. The landing was completed on the prompt rather than on SP's own judgment.
texts.2: SP, due to a round out started slightly high, allowed the aircraft to float briefly before contact. SP held the landing attitude instead of forcing the aircraft down, allowed the speed to decay and touched down between the 500 and 1000 feet standards from the projected touch down point. The float was managed correctly and without intervention.
texts.3: SP began the round out at the correct height, blended the power reduction with the pitch change and established the landing attitude before contact. The aircraft touched down within 500 feet of the projected touch down point with no ballooning and no bounce. The transition from the approach attitude to the landing attitude was continuous and smooth.
texts.4: SP flew the round out with no discernible float and placed the aircraft on the runway in the correct landing attitude at the projected touch down point. The pitch change and the power reduction were blended so precisely that the descent rate was arrested exactly at the touch down height. Landings were repeated with the same result.

The trend indicates that the round out is being started marginally high and that the power reduction is trailing the pitch change. error_modes.label: Drift and crosswind correction at touch down

texts.0: SP, due to attention being captured entirely by the airspeed indication during the visual segment, did not monitor the lateral picture or remove the crosswind drift before touch down. The aircraft landed with drift, displaced more than 20 feet from the centerline and with the longitudinal axis off the runway heading, outside the plus/minus 15 feet limit. IP took the controls to correct the side load and to keep the aircraft on the runway.
texts.1: SP, due to fixation on one parameter during the round out, did not apply the crosswind correction until the point of touch down. The aircraft contacted the runway approximately 15 feet from the centerline with residual drift, at the limit, after IP called for rudder and into-wind aileron. texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the touch down point during the visual segment, initially left the crosswind drift uncorrected. SP recognized the lateral displacement developing, applied into-wind aileron and rudder and removed most of the drift before contact, touching down about 10 feet from the centerline, between the 5 and 15 feet standards. The correction was timely and required no intervention.
texts.3: SP divided attention correctly across the visual segment, applied the crosswind correction continuously and removed the drift before contact. Touch down occurred within 5 feet of the centerline with the longitudinal axis on the runway heading and no side load on the landing gear. Directional control was maintained positively through the rollout.
texts.4: SP established the crosswind correction early in the visual segment and adjusted it continuously as the wind effect changed near the surface. Touch down occurred within approximately 2 feet of the centerline with zero drift and the wings held level after contact. Scanning was distributed across attitude, alignment and speed without any parameter being neglected.
texts.marginal: SP corrected the drift within standards, but the crosswind correction was applied in a single late input rather than being carried through the visual segment. The trend shows attention narrowing onto the speed and the touch down point while the lateral picture is checked only intermittently. SP is expected to maintain a continuous scan of the runway alignment so that the drift is corrected progressively rather than removed at the last moment.

error_modes.label: Duck-under: correcting to the visual glide path with a high sink rate

The steep correction was never arrested, the aircraft arrived firmly well short of the projected touch down point and the touch down was more than 1000 feet from it. IP took the controls, added power and re-established a normal descent to the runway.
texts.1: SP, on acquiring the runway environment slightly high, pushed to the visual glide path with a sink rate far greater than a shallow correction requires. The rate was reduced only after a verbal prompt for power and the aircraft touched down short of the projected point by the full 1000 feet allowed for the standard. SP acknowledged the duck-under and flew the remaining pattern with a stabilized visual glide path.

The aim point stayed stable in the windscreen and the touch down was within 500 feet of the projected point. Power was adjusted early enough that the correction was never abrupt.
texts.4: SP joined the visual glide path with a barely perceptible change in descent rate and held the aim point fixed in the windscreen from break out to round out. error_modes.label: Transition started before adequate visual references were available

texts.0: SP started the transition to landing without adequate visual references of the runway environment available, going head up on the first glimpse of approach lights rather than adapting to the outside environment as the cues appeared. texts.2: SP transitioned outside a little early, with only partial visual references, and the crosscheck of the flight instruments thinned out before the picture was complete. A small drift built up unnoticed and the aircraft touched down about 10 feet off the centerline before SP corrected the tracking on the rollout. The lapse was recognized without prompting and the following approach was flown with a proper split of attention.
texts.3: SP kept the instrument crosscheck running until the runway environment provided adequate visual references, then adapted outside at the rate the cues appeared. No period was left without a primary source of aircraft control and the touch down was within 5 feet of the centerline. The changeover of attention was orderly.
texts.4: SP blended the instrument and visual references so that the transition was invisible from the back seat, with the crosscheck released only as each outside cue became reliable. Centerline tracking was essentially exact at touch down. At no point was the aircraft flown on an incomplete visual picture.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the standards, but the eyes went outside on the first approach light rather than on an adequate runway environment picture, and the instrument crosscheck was reduced earlier than it should have been. Deviations remained small only because the weather cleared quickly. SP is expected to hold the crosscheck until the visual references are genuinely adequate and then adapt outside at the rate the cues appear.

error_modes.label: Slowing to the transition speed of 105 KIAS (100 KIAS flaps LDG) with the field in sight

The excess energy produced a long float and the aircraft was still well above the allowed touch down speed band when it was forced onto the runway. IP intervened with power and pitch to control the arrival.

The float that followed put the touch down speed at the full 10 knots above the reference for the configuration flown. Verbal instruction was required to reduce power and stabilize the speed for landing.
texts.2: SP reduced power late after the decision to land, so the aircraft reached the transition speed only in the last part of the visual segment instead of settling on 105 KIAS, or 100 KIAS with flaps LDG, when the field came in sight. texts_above.2: SP recognized the residual energy, contained it without any prompting and completed a normal landing, after touch down had trended about 7 knots fast on the reference for the configuration flown. Reducing power the moment the decision to land is made, rather than in the last part of the visual segment, would remove most of that residual energy. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to assured speed-transition technique.
texts_above.3: SP slowed the aircraft to the transition speed for the configuration flown as soon as the field was in sight and held it into the round out, with touch down speed staying within the standard 5 knot band above the reference and power reduction timely and smooth. The only refinement available is to time the reduction the same way on every landing as consistently as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise speed-transition technique.
texts_above.4: SP set the transition speed of 105 KIAS, or 100 KIAS with flaps LDG selected, immediately on deciding to land and flew it with negligible variation to the round out, with touch down speed on the reference, within about 1 knot, and no float. There is little left to refine; the power reduction is already anticipated rather than reactive. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate speed-transition technique.

error_modes.label: Continuity between the instrument glide path and the visual glide path (VASI use)

texts.0: SP abandoned the instrument glide path on breaking out without establishing a visual glide path in its place, and did not use the VASI or the other visual glide path guidance available on the runway. With no glide path reference of either kind, the descent was flown on impression alone and the touch down was displaced from the projected point by more than the limits of the standard. IP took the controls to re-establish a proper descent path to the runway.
texts.1: SP left the instrument glide path indications behind before picking up the visual glide path guidance, so the aircraft flew a segment with no glide path reference at all. The VASI indication was consulted only after a verbal prompt and the touch down ended the full 1000 feet from the projected point. SP flew the following approach maintaining the instrument glide path until the visual guidance was established.
texts.2: SP maintained the instrument glide path but transferred to the visual glide path in a single step rather than overlapping the two references, and read the VASI late. The gap in guidance cost about 800 feet at the touch down point relative to the projection. SP recognized the discrepancy from the VASI and corrected the descent before the round out without any prompting.
texts.3: SP either maintained the instrument glide path to the round out or transitioned to a visual glide path with the two references overlapping, using the VASI as the technique recommends. The touch down was within 500 feet of the projected point. The change of reference did not disturb the descent.
texts.4: SP carried the instrument glide path indications until the visual glide path guidance was firmly established, so the descent path was continuous and the VASI stayed on the correct indication throughout. Displacement of the touch down from the projected point was negligible. The changeover was not detectable in the flight path.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the touch down point standards, but the instrument glide path was dropped a little before the visual glide path was solid and the VASI was used as a check rather than as guidance. The path remained acceptable mainly because the runway was familiar. SP is expected to overlap the two glide path references and to use the VASI or the other visual glide path guidance as the primary aid on the visual segment.

texts_at.0: SP flew the transition with the IP overlapping the instrument and visual glide path references on the first approach and calling the VASI indication for SP to read on the second. Overlapping the instrument and visual glide path references, rather than dropping one before picking up the other, has not yet been learned. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to overlap the glide path references independently as the technique becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP maintained glide path continuity with touch down settling at the full 1000 feet from the projected point, due to abandoning the instrument glide path on breaking out without establishing a visual glide path in its place. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start that overlap at the same point on every approach as consistently as the others.

error_modes.label: Continuing the landing after visual references degrade following the break out (ground fog)

texts.0: SP continued the landing after ground fog degraded the visual references that had been available at the break out, although the technique states that such weather phenomena may require a missed approach even after breaking out from IMC to VMC. With the runway environment lost and no return to the instruments, the aircraft ended up outside the limits of the standard in both touch down point and centerline tracking. IP took the controls and executed the missed approach.
texts.1: SP pressed on toward the runway as the references thinned out in the fog layer, reassessing neither the missed approach option nor the instrument glide path. Tracking degraded until the aircraft was at the full 15 feet from the centerline at touch down and the decision to go around was taken only after verbal instruction. SP acknowledged that the degradation of the references had been observed and not acted upon.
texts.2: SP recognized that the visual references were degrading in the shallow fog, but continued a few seconds longer before returning attention to the instruments to back up the visual picture. The delay showed as a drift of about 10 feet from the centerline at touch down, corrected on the rollout without prompting. The missed approach option was verbalized correctly, if late.
texts.3: SP monitored the quality of the visual references after the break out and, with the runway environment remaining usable, continued the landing while backing up the visual picture with the instruments. Deviations at touch down stayed within the standards for both centerline and touch down point. The missed approach criteria were stated and applied correctly.
texts.4: SP evaluated the visual references continuously through the visual segment and treated the fog layer as a live threat, with the missed approach decision briefed and ready. The landing was completed with negligible deviations because the references remained adequate throughout. The reassessment never disturbed aircraft control.
texts.marginal: SP landed within standards, but the thinning of the references in the fog was noted without any restatement of the missed approach criteria, and the decision to continue was made by default rather than deliberately. Deviations stayed inside the tolerance because the layer was shallow. SP is expected to reassess the missed approach option actively whenever a weather phenomenon degrades the references after the break out from IMC to VMC.

texts_at.0: SP flew the approach in ground fog with the IP restating the missed approach criteria on the first approach and calling the reassessment for SP to make on the second. Restating the missed approach criteria the instant the references begin to thin has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to restate the criteria and reassess independently as the judgement becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP continued the landing in ground fog with tracking degrading until the aircraft reached the full 15 feet from the centerline at touch down, due to pressing on toward the runway as the references thinned without reassessing the missed approach option or the instrument glide path. texts_at.2: SP continued the landing in the shallow fog with a drift of about 10 feet from the centerline at touch down, due to continuing a few seconds longer before returning attention to the instruments to back up the visual picture. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to restate those criteria at the same point on every approach with degraded references.

error_modes.label: Use of the reviewed airport data (runway lighting, dimensions, slope, obstructions) for the visual segment

texts.0: SP had not reviewed the airport diagram of the approach chart for runway lighting, runway dimensions, runway slope and charted obstructions, so the visual picture built at the break out was based on an assumed standard runway. The unfamiliar sight picture produced by the actual runway width and slope led to an aim point far from the intended one and to a touch down displaced beyond the limits of the standard. IP intervened to correct the flight path to the runway.
texts.1: SP flew the visual segment with no working knowledge of the runway dimensions and slope taken from the approach chart, and accepted a sight picture that did not match the projected touch down point. The aim point was corrected only after a verbal indication and the touch down was the full 1000 feet from the projected point. SP later identified the missing chart review as the cause.
texts.2: SP had reviewed the airport diagram only superficially and misread the sight picture created by the runway slope, aiming for a point noticeably beyond the intended one. The error was recognized against the runway markings and the aim point was adjusted before the round out, leaving the touch down about 800 feet from the projection. No prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP applied the reviewed runway data, lighting configuration, dimensions and slope to the visual segment, so the sight picture was interpreted correctly from the break out. The touch down was within 500 feet of the projected point. The aim point required only minor adjustment.
texts.4: SP had the airport diagram thoroughly reviewed and stated the runway dimensions, slope and lighting in the approach brief, so the sight picture at the break out matched the expectation exactly. Displacement of the touch down from the projected point was negligible. The charted obstructions were accounted for without any change of plan.
texts.marginal: SP touched down within standards, but the runway slope and lighting configuration were recalled only vaguely and the aim point was set by feel rather than from the reviewed airport data. The result was acceptable because the sight picture happened to be close to the familiar one. SP is expected to review the airport diagram for lighting, dimensions, slope and charted obstructions before flight and to use that data to build the visual picture.

texts_at.0: SP flew the visual segment with the IP reviewing the airport diagram for lighting, dimensions and slope before flight on the first approach and calling the aim point for SP to fly on the second. Reviewing the airport diagram before flight, so the sight picture at break out matches expectation, has not yet been learned. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to review the airport diagram and build the sight picture independently as the technique becomes familiar.
